text: # Rocket Landing Lab A local deep reinforcement learning lab that trains PPO to land a rocket, demonstrates reward hacking, and evaluates reliability across weather conditions. Built with Python, Gymnasium, Stable-Baselines3, PyTorch, FastAPI, scikit-learn, SQLite and a local Ollama assistant. Inspired by Hari (@harixganesh)'s Lunar Lander reward-shaping project. Implementation developed with AI assistance. ## New: guided browser lab Double-click **Open-Web-Lab.cmd** after setup. Start with the beginner introduction, then explore telemetry analytics, flight replay, a supervised failure predictor, a local RAG assistant, and randomized-weather PPO training. Includes 720 recorded flights and measured predictor results. The older desktop panel remains available. Read the [web lab and placement supplement](docs/WEB-LAB.md) for architecture, demonstration steps, concepts, evaluation and limitations. The predictor has 77.8% held-out accuracy but only 21.7% failure recall; it is not a dependable crash alarm. Local generated answers use Ollama with `qwen3:1.7b`; without it the assistant shows retrieved evidence. ![Rocket Landing Lab introduction](docs/web-lab-preview.png) ## Features - Four saved policies: original reward, time penalty, deliberate hover exploit and corrected progress shaping. - Desktop controls for watching, recording and evaluating flights. - Calm, breezy and gusty stress tests with confidence intervals and CSV exports. - Automated quality gate: sample size, landing reliability, timeouts, original score and model identity. - Repeatable evaluation seeds, model checksums and

Select a final model and click **Watch AI**. Four small trained models are included, so retraining is optional. Setup needs internet access; installed inference runs locally on CPU. GIF recording is included. text: # Web lab: demonstration and placement preparation This guide covers the version 3 additions. Read it alongside the original placement PDF, which describes the original PPO and reward-shaping project. All results here are from a simulator, not a physical rocket. ## Start and demonstrate 1. Double-click `Open-Web-Lab.cmd`. Keep its console window open while using the app. The launcher chooses an available local port and opens your browser. Close the console to stop the server. 2. Start on the introduction: explain the eight observations, four discrete actions, feedback through rewards, and the deliberately flawed hovering policy. 3. Enter the lab. Overview compares saved policies. Filter by weather and inspect the number of flights, landing rate, original score, and simulated duration. Export the filtered records as CSV. 4. Open Flight explorer. Search for `hover`, `failed`, a weather condition, or a seed. Play or scrub the reconstructed trajectory and inspect speed, tilt, and engine actions. The drawing is schematic, not a new video rendered by Box2D. 5. Open Failure predictor. Explain why a classifier is a separate model from the PPO controller. Scikit-learn supplies preprocessing, classifiers, metrics and text retrieval. Joblib stores the fitted classifier. PyPDF reads the placement PDF for retrieval. Gymnasium/Box2D supplies the environment; Stable-Baselines3/PyTorch supplies PPO training and inference. Matplotlib remains responsible for the original experiment reports. Filtering outcomes conditions the statistics: selecting only landed flights necessarily displays 100% landing rate. Compare policies with the same weather, seed set, and outcome filter. The 95% Wilson interval estimates uncertainty in a binomial landing proportion, not variation across training seeds. Shared seed numbers help comparisons but weather changes can alter random draws and trajectories. ## Failure predictor: supervised learning without looking into the future The target is one of `failed`, `landed`, `timeout`. The forecast is made at step 150, or three seconds. Flights ending by that point are excluded: their outcome is already known. There are 714 eligible flights and six excluded early endings in the included dataset. For x, y, vx, vy, angle and angular speed, compute last value, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum over observations 0–150. Add main-engine and side-engine fractions from actions 1–150. This produces 32 features. The input deliberately excludes final return, final length, weather label, policy name, final outcome and observations after step 150. The final outcome is used only as the supervised target. Split by episode seed group, keeping every policy/weather version of the same seed

text: minimum and maximum over observations 0–150. Add main-engine and side-engine fractions from actions 1–150. This produces 32 features. The input deliberately excludes final return, final length, weather label, policy name, final outcome and observations after step 150. The final outcome is used only as the supervised target. Split by episode seed group, keeping every policy/weather version of the same seed in one partition. GroupShuffleSplit first holds out 20% of groups for testing, then 25% of remaining groups for validation (approximately 60/20/20 overall). Fit a standard-scaled logistic regression and a random forest on training data only. Choose the model with the highest validation macro F1. Do not refit or select using the test set. The included selected model is a random forest; all split seed lists and per-flight assignments are saved. Held-out results: accuracy 77.78%, macro F1 0.668, landing Brier score 0.162 on 144 flights. The confusion matrix has actual rows and predicted columns in the order failed/landed/timeout: | Actual | Predicted failed | Predicted landed | Predicted timeout | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Failed | 5 | 18 | 0 | | Landed | 4 | 73 | 5 | | Timeout | 0 | 5 | 34 | This exposes a significant limitation: failure recall is only 5/23 = 21.7%. Accuracy alone conceals it. The predictor is an educational diagnostic, not a reliable crash alarm. Macro F1 weighs the three classes equally; Brier score measures squared probability error for landing, with lower being better. The reliability table compares predicted probability and observed landing frequency. Probabilities are not guaranteed to be calibrated. No threshold was tuned on the test data. Replay labels each flight as train, validation, test or new; an individual training-flight prediction is not independent evidence of performance. Generalization is to unseen seed groups for the known policies, not unseen algorithms or real rockets. Adding policies, changing feature definitions or repeatedly consulting the test set requires a new evaluation protocol. A policy-held-out split and additional training seeds are useful future research. Model file hashing detects accidental inconsistency with the report; it does not authenticate untrusted files. Only load the repository's locally produced Joblib artifacts. ## RAG: retrieval augmented generation The assistant reads project documentation, PDF pages, Python source, and original quality-gate facts. It splits text into overlapping 210-word windows with a 150-word stride. Each chunk retains its file/page and source ID. TF-IDF with word unigrams and bigrams builds a sparse index. The question is transformed using the same vectorizer; cosine-like normalized dot products rank chunks. Up to four chunks with similarity above 0.055 become context. This is lexical retrieval, not neural embeddings or a vector database. That is a valid, small local RAG baseline, but synonyms and complex questions may retrieve weak evidence. Ollama serves the local Qwen3 1.7B model. The prompt asks it to use supplied evidence, admit insufficient support, and cite source IDs. The app shows retrieved excerpts and file/page identifiers so users can inspect the grounding. The assistant does not control the rocket, run arbitrary commands, or modify training from its text response. Four vectorized environments feed PPO. It continues learning with the original reward only, preserving the source checkpoint. The explicit new training seed controls Python/NumPy/PyTorch and environment seeds after loading the source model. PPO collects full rollout batches, so 200,000 requested steps produce 200,704 additional steps with this configuration. Source and additional step counts are recorded separately. The final checkpoint goes into a new `runs/robust/seed_N` folder; `config.json` records source hash, weather ranges, reward and seed. Interrupted training folders may lack a final checkpoint and are not collected as policies. text: tested for 50 episodes in each of calm, breezy and gusty weather, seed numbers 700000–700049. The results page reports original return, landing rate and Wilson intervals. This is an exploratory comparison of two saved policies. Continued learning can improve one condition and degrade another. It also changes both weather exposure and reward relative to the source's original training, so improvements cannot be attributed solely to weather randomization. Strong causal evidence requires controlled ablations, multiple training seeds and a final untouched test set. Reusing these evaluation seeds for iterative tuning turns them into development data. The corrected seeded run (seed 2, 200,704 additional steps) produced the following 50-episode rates: source vs new policy was 90% vs 92% calm, 92% vs 88% breezy, and 68% vs 76% gusty. Gusty mean original score increased from 141.6 to 159.4, while breezy declined from 217.0 to 201.5. These are observed differences with overlapping uncertainty intervals, not proof of a general improvement. An initial implementation check revealed a seed-reset issue and was archived; the corrected run was not chosen by ranking training runs. Interest mapping: AI/ML covers control and classification; deep learning covers the PPO neural policy and local language model; RAG covers retrieval and grounded explanations; data analytics covers telemetry, filtering, exports, uncertainty and comparison.
